title: At the supra table
goal: Survive — and enjoy — a Georgian feast: understand the tamada's role, answer toasts, praise your hosts, and turn down seconds without offending anyone.
bekal: understand what happens at a supra
praise the food and the hosts
politely turn down a drink or more food
say thank you the Georgian way when leaving

dialogs.title: დიალოგი — A first supra
dialogs.intro: Ani is invited to dinner at Nino's family home in Kakheti. The table is full before everyone has even sat down. Nino's uncle, Zurab, acts as the თამადა — the head of the table.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Thank you so much. The table is beautiful.

lines.speaker: ზურაბი:
lines.id: I'm the tamada. The first toast — to peace!
lines.literal: I — head-of-table — am. first — toast — peace-to!

lines.speaker: ზურაბი:
lines.id: The second toast — to our guests! A guest is a gift from God.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: I'm very grateful. Everything is delicious.
lines.literal: very — grateful — I-am. everything — very — tasty-is.

lines.speaker: ზურაბი:
lines.id: Have some more! You've eaten so little!

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Thank you, but I really can't. I don't drink wine, sorry.
lines.literal: thank-you, but — really — can't — I-will-manage. wine-object — not — I-drink, sorry.

lines.speaker: ზურაბი:
lines.id: That's okay! Drink with water — it's the heart that matters, not the wine.
lines.literal: not — bad-to-it! water-with — drink — heart — main-is, not — wine.

lines.speaker: ანი:
lines.id: Thank you for everything. I've never been a guest like this before.
lines.literal: thank-you — everything-for. like-this — guest-visit — never — I-have-had.

notes: **A სუფრა (supra) is more than just dinner.** It's a feast with rules: one person leads (**თამადა**, tamada), toasts are made in a set order of themes — peace, guests, parents, those who have passed away, children, the homeland, women — and no one drinks outside a toast. The table is never empty; new dishes arrive stacked on top of the old ones.

**გაუმარჯოს = "victory to it/them".** ⚠️ This isn't "cheers", and it isn't said casually. It's said by the tamada or whoever is giving the toast; **guests just repeat it and drink**. As a foreigner, no one expects a speech from you — until you want to give one, and then everyone will go quiet and listen.

**სტუმარი ღვთისაა — "a guest is a gift from God".** The proverb that explains almost all of Georgian hospitality. It's the source of a habit that often confuses foreigners: hosts will give more than they can afford, and turning everything down actually hurts.

**Turning down a drink is fine, and there's a right way to do it.** ⚠️ Don't cover your glass with your hand or refuse with a flat *არა*. What works: **ღვინოს არ ვსვამ** (I don't drink wine) — give a reason if you like (religion, health, driving), then **წყლით დავლევ** (I'll toast with water). Toasting with water or lemonade is completely accepted; what isn't accepted is not joining in at all.

**If you don't drink alcohol, say so at the start, not halfway through.** The full sentence: *ბოდიში, ალკოჰოლს არ ვსვამ — რელიგიის გამო* (sorry, I don't drink alcohol — for religious reasons). In Georgia this is understood without argument; the country has lived beside Muslim neighbors for centuries, and it has a sizable Muslim population of its own in Adjara.

**მიირთვი / მიირთვით = "please, help yourself".** A polite form of "eat" used especially with guests, and you'll hear it dozens of times in one evening. A good enough reply: *მადლობა, ძალიან გემრიელია.*

**Praising the hosts matters more than praising the food.** The sentences that really stay with people: *ასეთი სტუმრობა არასდროს მქონია* (I've never been a guest like this before) and *თქვენი ოჯახი ძალიან სტუმართმოყვარეა* (your family is so hospitable).

after: **ალავერდი** is when the tamada hands the turn to toast to someone else. If your name is called, one short sentence is more than enough: *მადლობა ყველაფრისთვის. ამ ოჯახს გაუმარჯოს!* — and the whole table will applaud.

after: **გენაცვალე** literally means something like "let me take your place" — a declaration that the speaker is willing to bear whatever befalls you. It's used every day, with children, guests, even customers at the market. No other language has an exact equivalent.

sections.title: Surviving a supra: six practical things

blocks.title: What to know before you sit down
items: **Don't drink before there's a toast.** Glasses are raised only when a sadghegrdzelo is given. Sipping wine in between is seen as odd, not relaxed.
**Beer isn't used for toasting.** In Georgia, toasting with beer has a bad meaning — it's used to remember enemies. If you're holding a beer, raise a glass of water for the toast instead.
**Don't clean your plate to show good manners.** An empty plate means you're still hungry, and it will be refilled right away. Leaving a little is the signal that you've had enough.
**Praise the people, not just the food.** *ვინ მოამზადა?* (who cooked this?) followed by thanking that person directly means far more than praising the taste.
**Saying goodbye takes time.** Standing up and leaving right away is considered rude. Set aside fifteen minutes to say goodbye, and thank your hosts in person.
**If you don't drink alcohol, say so at the start, once, calmly.** After that it won't come up again, and your glass will be filled with lemonade or water without a single comment.

blocks.text: One thing is hard to prepare for with memorized sentences: a supra can last five hours, and the hosts will keep giving. What visitors often get wrong is treating it as a polite ritual to be refused again and again — in Georgia the offer is real, and refusing repeatedly only makes the hosts try harder. The way out that works best is to accept a little, praise sincerely, then stop calmly: *მადლობა, საკმარისია.*

And one thing you may carry home longer than the vocabulary. Toasting in Georgia is not a game; it follows an order, it's sincere, and it almost always mentions those who are gone and those not yet born. If someone raises a glass to **ინდონეზიას** (Indonesia — or your own country) and says your name in it, that isn't mere politeness. There's only one fitting answer, and now you know the words: **გმადლობთ. თქვენს ოჯახს გაუმარჯოს!**
